studies.title: A transdiagnostic neuroanatomical signature of psychiatric illness.
studies.abstract: Despite an increasing focus on transdiagnostic approaches to mental health, it remains unclear whether different diagnostic categories share a common neuronatomical basis. The current investigation sought to investigate whether a transdiagnostic set of structural alterations characterized schizophrenia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and determine whether any such alterations reflected markers of psychiatric illness or pre-existing familial vulnerability. A total of 404 patients with a psychiatric diagnosis were recruited (psychosis, n = 129; unipolar depression, n = 92; post-traumatic stress disorder, n = 91; obsessive-compulsive disorder, n = 92) alongside n = 201 healthy controls and n = 20 unaffected first-degree relatives. We collected structural magnetic resonance imaging scans from each participant, and tested for transdiagnostic alterations using Voxel-based morphometry. Inferences were made at p < 0.05 after family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons. The four psychiatric groups relative to healthy controls were all characterized by significantly greater gray matter volume in the putamen (right: z-score: 5.97, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 4.97, p-value = 0.001); the volume of this region was positively correlated with severity of symptoms across groups (r = 0.313; p < 0.001). Putamen enlargement was also evident in unaffected relatives compared to healthy controls (right: z-score: 8.13, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 9.38, p-value < 0.001). Taken collectively, these findings indicate that increased putamen volume may reflect a transdiagnostic marker of familial vulnerability to psychopathology. This is consistent with emerging conceptualizations of psychiatric illness, in which each disorder is understood as a combination of diagnosis-specific features and a transdiagnostic factor reflecting general psychopathology.

studies.title: Frontal and subcortical grey matter reductions in PTSD.
studies.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterised by a range of debilitating psychological, physical and cognitive symptoms. PTSD has been associated with grey matter atrophy in limbic and frontal cortical brain regions. However, previous studies have reported heterogeneous findings, with grey matter changes observed beyond limbic/frontal areas. Seventy-five adults were recruited from the community, 25 diagnosed with PTSD along with 25 healthy and 25 trauma exposed age and gender matched controls. Participants underwent clinical assessment and magnetic resonance imaging. The data-analyses method Voxel Based Morphometry (VBM) was used to estimate cortical grey matter volumes. When compared to both healthy and trauma exposed controls, PTSD subjects demonstrated decreased grey matter volumes within subcortical brain regions-including the hippocampus and amygdala-along with reductions in the anterior cingulate cortex, frontal medial cortex, middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, paracingulate gyrus, and precuneus cortex. Significant negative correlations were found between total CAPS lifetime clinical scores/sub-scores and GM volume of both the PTSD and TC groups. GM volumes of the left rACC and right amygdala showed a significant negative correlation within PTSD diagnosed subjects.

studies.title: Duration of posttraumatic stress disorder predicts hippocampal grey matter loss.
studies.abstract: To examine the impact of environmental stress on grey matter volume in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), we investigated the relationship between duration of PTSD and grey matter volume of hippocampus and anterior cingulate cortex. Twenty-one participants with PTSD and 17 trauma-exposed controls, matched for age and sex and with no history of substance dependence, underwent a T1-weighted structural MRI scan and voxel-based morphometry was employed. After controlling for age, depression and whole-brain volume, analysis of covariance revealed significant reductions in hippocampus and rostral anterior cingulate cortex in PTSD, and there was a significant negative correlation between right hippocampal volume and PTSD duration. This pattern suggests that prolonged PTSD may have cumulative adverse effects on hippocampal volume, highlighting the potential role of genetic-environmental interactions.

studies.title: Structural brain abnormalities common to posttraumatic stress disorder and depression.
studies.abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and major depression are reliably associated with reductions in brain volume in markedly similar areas. studies.title: Effects of post-traumatic stress disorder on occipital lobe function and structure.
studies.abstract: Although there is evidence for strong connectivity between the amygdala and the visual cortex and some evidence for reduced occipital lobe gray matter volume in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), few studies have directly examined the effects of PTSD on occipital function. The current study used functional and structural MRI to examine occipital cortex function and structure in male combat veterans with and without PTSD. Left occipital gray matter volume was reduced in PTSD patients relative to the controls and correlated negatively with the severity of PTSD symptoms. Functional activity in the lateral occipital complex to aversive and nonaversive pictures presented in novel and repeated presentations was not altered by PTSD. These findings suggest that PTSD adversely affects occipital lobe volume but not the reactivity of the lateral occipital complex to generally aversive, trauma nonspecific stimuli.

studies.title: Structure of orbitofrontal cortex and its longitudinal course in cancer-related post-traumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: The neurobiological basis of cancer-related post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has never been studied. We investigated brain structural alterations and the longitudinal courses in patients with cancer-related PTSD. Baseline scans using magnetic resonance imaging were performed in 14 cancer survivors with PTSD, 100 without PTSD, and 70 healthy subjects. Follow-up scans were performed 2 years later in 76 cancer survivors (PTSD, n=9; non-PTSD, n=67). Using voxel-based morphometry, the gray matter volume (GMV) of the cancer survivors with PTSD was compared with the GMVs of those without PTSD and of the healthy subjects. The effects of the interactions between the diagnosis and the timing of the GMV measurements were examined. The GMV of the right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) was significantly smaller in cancer survivors with PTSD than in those without PTSD or healthy subjects. The interaction between the diagnosis and the timing of the right OFC's GMV measurement was not significant. The OFC, which is thought to be involved in the extinction of fear conditioning and the retrieval of emotional memory, might play an important role in the pathophysiology of PTSD. Moreover, the OFC's GMV may remain constant after the development of cancer-related PTSD.

studies.title: Voxel-based analysis of MRI reveals anterior cingulate gray-matter volume reduction in posttraumatic stress disorder due to terrorism.
studies.abstract: MRI studies using the manual tracing method have shown a smaller-than-normal hippocampal volume in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, these studies have yielded inconsistent results, and brain structures other than the hippocampus have not been well investigated. A recently developed, fully automated method called voxel-based morphometry enables an exploration of structural changes throughout the brain by applying statistical parametric mapping to high-resolution MRI. Here we first used this technology in patients with PTSD. Participants were 9 victims of the Tokyo subway sarin attack with PTSD and 16 matched victims of the same traumatic event without PTSD. The voxel-based morphometry showed a significant gray-matter volume reduction in the left anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in trauma survivors with PTSD compared with those without PTSD. The severity of the disorder was negatively correlated with the gray-matter volume of the left ACC in PTSD subjects. There were no significant differences in other gray-matter regions or any of the white-matter regions between two groups. The present study demonstrates evidence for structural abnormalities of ACC in patients with PTSD. Together with previous functional neuroimaging studies showing a dysfunction of this region, the present findings provide further support for the important role of ACC, which is pivotally involved in attention, emotional regulation, and conditioned fear, in the pathology of PTSD.

studies.title: Post-traumatic stress symptoms correlate with smaller subgenual cingulate, caudate, and insula volumes in unmedicated combat veterans.
studies.abstract: Prior studies have examined differences in brain volume between patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and control subjects. Convergent findings include smaller hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex volumes in PTSD. However, post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) exist on a spectrum, and neural changes may occur beyond the diagnostic threshold of PTSD. We examined the relationship between PTSS and gray matter among combat-exposed U.S. military veterans. Structural brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained on 28 combat veterans from Operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. PTSS were assessed using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS). Thirteen subjects met criteria for PTSD. Subjects were unmedicated, and free of major comorbid psychiatric disorders. Images were analyzed using voxel-based morphometry, and regressed against the total CAPS score and trauma load. Images were subsequently analyzed by diagnosis of PTSD vs. non-PTSD. CAPS scores were inversely correlated with volumes of the subgenual cingulate (sgACC), caudate, hypothalamus, insula, and left middle temporal gyrus (MTG). studies.title: Gray matter density in limbic and paralimbic cortices is associated with trauma load and EMDR outcome in PTSD patients.
studies.abstract: There is converging evidence of gray matter (GM) structural alterations in different limbic structures in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) patients. The aim of this study was to evaluate GM density in PTSD in relation to trauma load, and to assess the GM differences between responders (R) and non-responders (NR) to EMDR therapy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans of 21 subjects exposed to occupational trauma, who developed PTSD (S), and of 22 who did not (NS), were compared by means of an optimized Voxel-Based Morphometry (VBM) analysis as implemented in SPM. Within S, further comparisons were made between 10 R and 5 NR. A regression analysis between GM density and the Traumatic Antecedents Questionnaire (TAQ) was also performed on all 43 subjects. Results showed a significantly lower GM density in S as compared to NS in the left posterior cingulate and the left posterior parahippocampal gyrus. Moreover, NR showed a significantly lower GM density as compared to R in bilateral posterior cingulate, as well as anterior insula, anterior parahippocampal gyrus and amygdala in the right hemisphere. Regression analysis showed that GM density negatively correlated with trauma load in bilateral posterior cingulate, left anterior insula, and right anterior parahippocampal gyrus. In conclusion, a GM lower density in limbic and paralimbic cortices were found to be associated with PTSD diagnosis, trauma load, and EMDR treatment outcome, suggesting a view of PTSD characterized by memory and dissociative disturbances.

studies.title: Evidence of diffuse damage in frontal and occipital cortex in the brain of patients with post-traumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: A number of MRI studies have shown focal or diffuse cortical gray matter (GM) abnormalities in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, the results of these studies are unclear regarding the cortical regions involved in this condition, perhaps due to the heterogeneity of the PTSD population included or to the differences in the methodology used for the quantification of the brain structures. In this study, we assessed differences in cortical GM volumes between a selected group of 25 drug-naive PTSD patients with history of adulthood trauma and 25 matched non-traumatized controls. Analyses were performed by using two different automated methods: the structural image evaluation using normalization of atrophy (SIENAX) and the voxel-based morphometry (VBM), as we trusted that if these complementary techniques provided similar results, it would increase the confidence in the validity of the assessment. Results of SIENAX and VBM analyses similarly showed that cortical GM volume decreases in PTSD patients when compared to healthy controls, particularly in the frontal and occipital lobes. These decreases seem to correlate with clinical measures. Our findings suggest that in drug-naïve PTSD patients with a history of adulthood trauma, brain structural damage is diffuse, with a particular prevalence for the frontal and occipital lobes, and is clinically relevant.

studies.title: Gray matter density reduction in the insula in fire survivors with posttraumatic stress disorder: a voxel-based morphometric study.
studies.abstract: Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) is an objective whole-brain technique for characterizing regional cerebral volume and tissue concentration differences in structural magnetic resonance images. In the current study, we used VBM to examine possible cerebral gray matter abnormalities in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) due to fire. The subjects included 12 victims of a fire disaster with PTSD and 12 matched victims of the same fire without PTSD. Magnetic resonance images were obtained on a 1.5-Tesla General Electric scanner at Central South University, and an entire brain volume of 248 contiguous slices was obtained for each subject. Then, gray matter density in patients with PTSD and control groups was compared by using a VBM approach in SPM2. Group analysis was thresholded at P<0.001, uncorrected, at the voxel level. The following three regions of reduced gray matter volume were found in patients with PTSD compared with controls: left hippocampus, left anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and bilateral insular cortex. It was concluded that there are structural abnormalities of the hippocampus, the ACC and the insular cortex in patients with PTSD due to fire.

studies.title: Decreased gray matter volume in the left hippocampus and bilateral calcarine cortex in coal mine flood disaster survivors with recent onset PTSD.
studies.abstract: Although limbic structure changes have been found in chronic and recent onset post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients, there are few studies about brain structure changes in recent onset PTSD patients after a single extreme and prolonged trauma. In the current study, 20 coal mine flood disaster survivors underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and region of interest (ROI) techniques were used to detect the gray matter and white matter volume changes in 10 survivors with recent onset PTSD and 10 survivors without PTSD. The correlation between the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS) and gray matter density in the ROI was also studied. Compared with survivors without PTSD, survivors with PTSD had significantly decreased gray matter volume and density in left anterior hippocampus, left parahippocampal gyrus, and bilateral calcarine cortex. The CAPS score correlated negatively with the gray matter density in bilateral calcarine cortex and left hippocampus in coal mine disaster survivors. Our study suggests that the gray matter volume and density of limbic structure decreased in recent onset PTSD patients who were exposed to extreme trauma. PTSD symptom severity was associated with gray matter density in calcarine cortex and hippocampus.

Exclusion criteria met: E4 (the study reports only region-based morphometry/ROI analyses with no qualifying whole-brain VBM results) and E7 (morphometry was performed using non-voxel-based RBM/region-based measures with no voxel-wise VBM contrast). Inclusion criteria satisfied: I3 (empirical English-language MRI study assessing gray matter volume differences between PTSD patients and controls), I6 (control groups include healthy and trauma-exposed individuals), I7 (adult sample). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise GM contrast reported). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion provided). Therefore the paper must be excluded from a meta-analysis that requires whole-brain VBM contrasts.

This study is an empirical English-language MRI study of adult PTSD patients vs controls using both manual volumetry and voxel-based morphometry (VBM) with voxel-wise, whole-brain two-sample t-tests (SPM2). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (MRI GM volume study), I4 (whole-brain voxel-wise between-group VBM contrast reported), I5 (results reported in main text), I6 (healthy control group), I7 (adult sample). However, the paper reports only null between-group results (no significant GM differences by VBM or manual volumetry). Per exclusion criterion E11 (studies that report only null results), this study must be excluded from the meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria not met: none (all relevant inclusion criteria I3,I4,I5,I6,I7 are satisfied). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using optimized voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare gray matter density between 21 adult PTSD patients and 22 trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (NS > S and R > NR) with cluster-level correction and provides Talairach coordinates and tables/figures of results. Controls are trauma-exposed non-PTSD adults. An adult working cohort is described. Although the paper includes an EMDR treatment subset, the main between-group PTSD vs trauma-exposed control VBM contrasts satisfy the meta-analysis requirements.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study reporting gray-matter volumetric comparisons between PTSD and control groups (meets I3) using healthy nonmaltreated controls (meets I6). However, it is a pediatric sample of children and adolescents (explicitly described as maltreated children and adolescents with PTSD), violating adult-sample requirement (E6). The morphometry used manual, ROI-based volumetric tracing of the superior temporal gyrus rather than whole-brain voxel-wise (VBM) analyses, violating the requirement for whole-brain voxel-wise GM contrasts (I4) and matching exclusion for ROI-only/non-voxel-based methods (E4 and E7). Therefore it does not provide the necessary whole-brain voxel-wise GM between-group contrasts among adults required for inclusion.

This is an empirical English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (SPM5 with DARTEL) comparing gray matter volume between adult PTSD patients and trauma-exposed controls. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (FDR-corrected p<0.05) showing significant GM reductions (ventral premotor cortex and pregenual anterior cingulate), with results described in text and figures; ROI analyses for hippocampus/amygdala are also reported but whole-brain results are present. Both groups are trauma-exposed adults (recruited from outpatient clinic and university employees), and PTSD diagnosis was established with SCID. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the morphometry PTSD meta-analysis are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is an empirical MRI morphometry study in English that reports gray matter volume differences between PTSD patients and controls using both ROI and voxel-based morphometry (VBM). The abstract and results describe significant voxel clusters for group affiliation in the right hippocampus from a multiple regression VBM model (a whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrast), and ROI analyses reported decreased hippocampal volumes. Controls were healthy individuals. Participants are described as patients and controls consistent with adult clinical samples; absence of explicit ages in the available content does not preclude inclusion by the review rules. However, the provided full-text content appears incomplete (primarily abstract, metadata, and references rather than full methods/results/discussion), so I flagged fulltext_incomplete=true and assigned moderate confidence.

This is an empirical, English-language VBM MRI study of adult combat veterans with PTSD vs trauma-exposed controls (meets I3, I6, I7). However, the analysis is an ROI-based VBM approach: authors extracted eigenvariates from a priori olfactory ROIs and report ANCOVAs on those ROIs rather than presenting a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast. The paper does not report qualifying whole-brain voxel-wise GM volume contrasts of PTSD patients vs controls, so it fails I4 and meets exclusion criterion E4 (ROI-only results with no whole-brain results). Therefore the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical adult MRI study reporting grey-matter volume differences between PTSD patients and controls (meets I3) and reports VBM cluster coordinates/figures (meets I5). Controls include trauma-exposed and nontraumatized groups (meets I6), and all participants are adults (meets I7). However, the voxel-based morphometry analyses were performed with ROI masking based on FreeSurfer parcellation rather than as an unrestricted whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast. The paper does not report an unmasked whole-brain voxel-wise GM contrast of PTSD vs controls, so it fails inclusion criterion I4. Because only ROI-masked VBM (i.e., ROI-only voxel-wise results) are reported with no qualifying whole-brain voxel-wise results, exclusion criterion E4 applies. Therefore the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical English MRI study of adult PTSD patients and healthy controls that reports gray-matter and subcortical volumes using SIENAX and FSL FIRST (I3, I6, I7 met). However, the study does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise (VBM) between-group contrasts or coordinate-based results. Morphometry was performed using non–voxel-based methods (global GM/TBV measures and subcortical segmentation/ROI volumes) and no voxel-wise statistical maps or coordinates are provided. Therefore it fails the required whole-brain voxel-wise evidence criterion (I4 not met) and meets exclusion criteria E4 (only ROI/non–whole-brain results) and E7 (non-voxel-based morphometry only). Full text appears complete. Exclusion summary: (a) exclusion IDs met: E4, E7; (b) inclusion IDs met: I3, I6, I7; (c) inclusion IDs not met: I4. Consequently the study should be excluded from the voxel-wise GM meta-analysis.

This is an empirical, English-language MRI study comparing gray-matter volumes between adult PTSD patients (drug-naïve, mean age ~38, trauma in adulthood) and matched healthy controls, using both SIENAX and a VBM-style (voxel-wise) whole-brain analysis. The paper reports voxel-wise between-group contrasts (FSL-VBM 'randomize' permutations, cluster corrected results) with tables/figures of significant clusters (frontal and occipital decreases), satisfying whole-brain VBM reporting. Control group are healthy individuals. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so the full text is complete. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, pediatric sample, non-voxel-only methods, non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets all listed inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6, I7) and should be included in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare grey-matter volume between adult PTSD patients and controls (survivors of the same trauma without PTSD). The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts with peak Talairach coordinates and T-scores for regions showing reduced GM in PTSD (bilateral insula, left medial frontal gyrus), satisfying availability of coordinate tables/figures. Both groups are adults (mean ages ~33). Controls are trauma-exposed non-PTSD individuals (acceptable). Full text includes background, methods (VBM, fMRI), results (coordinates), and discussion, so the full text appears complete. Therefore all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 are met; no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical, peer-reviewed English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare grey matter volume between recent-onset PTSD patients and control groups. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (PTSD vs controls and non-PTSD vs controls) with family-wise error correction and cluster extent thresholds, and presents regional results (figures/tables) consistent with whole-brain analyses. Control groups include both trauma-exposed non-PTSD survivors and non-trauma-exposed healthy controls. Participants are adult male miners (adult sample). The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria are met (e.g., not ROI-only, not pediatric, reports significant between-group whole-brain results).

This is an empirical, peer-reviewed adult human MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare gray matter density between combat-exposed PTSD patients and controls (combat-exposed without PTSD and their unexposed cotwins). The full text includes background, methods (VBM whole-brain analyses with smoothing, SPM, small-volume corrections), results (voxel-wise between-group contrasts with peak coordinates, tables, and figures), and discussion. It reports whole-brain voxel-wise PTSD vs control contrasts and significant loci (hippocampus, pregenual ACC, insula) with coordinates and small-volume-corrected p-values. Controls are trauma-exposed and unexposed veterans (acceptable). Sample comprises adult Vietnam veterans. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, I7 and violates no exclusion criteria. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This is an empirical, adult, English MRI study comparing PTSD patients to healthy controls and reports global gray matter volumetric differences and hippocampal ROI volumes, but it does NOT report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast (e.g., VBM) of gray-matter volume. Exclusion criteria met: E4 (only ROI analyses / no qualifying whole‑brain results) and E7 (morphometry performed by non‑voxel‑based methods only: manual hippocampal tracing and global SIENAX volumes rather than voxel‑wise GM contrasts). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (empirical MRI study assessing GM volume differences), I6 (healthy control population), I7 (adult sample). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (no whole‑brain voxel-wise between-group GM contrast reported). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore excluded because the paper lacks the required whole‑brain voxel-wise GM contrast required by the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical, English-language adult MRI study that reports manual ROI volumetry (amygdala/hippocampus) comparing trauma-exposed adults with and without PTSD and also reports voxel-based morphometry (VBM) processing/correlational analyses. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (empirical MRI GM volume comparison), I5 (results reported in main text/figures), I6 (trauma-exposed controls without PTSD acceptable), I7 (adult sample). However, the paper does NOT report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group (PTSD vs controls) VBM contrast of grey-matter volume; the VBM work reported are correlational voxel-wise analyses and covariate/interactions rather than a direct whole-brain PTSD vs control GM contrast. Therefore it fails I4 and meets exclusion E4 (ROI analyses with no qualifying whole-brain between-group results). Full text appears complete. Conclusion: EXCLUDE for meta-analysis because no qualifying whole-brain PTSD vs control voxel-wise GM contrast was reported.

This is an empirical MRI study using voxel-based morphometry and SPM reporting whole-brain voxel-wise GM volume contrasts between PTSD and controls (I3, I4). Results (coordinates/figures) are presented (I5). Controls are healthy matched individuals (I6). However, the sample is pediatric (subjects ages 7–14; explicitly described as children/adolescents), so it fails the adult sample requirement (I7) and thus meets exclusion criterion E6 (pediatric study). Therefore the study must be excluded from this meta-analysis focused on adult PTSD morphometry.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study of adults with acute PTSD (ages 18–65) versus matched healthy controls that reports whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) between-group contrasts with coordinates and corrected p-values, assessing gray-matter differences. Volumetric analyses are also reported. The full text (background, methods, results, discussion) is available. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, non-voxel methods only, pediatric sample) apply.

Although this is an empirical, adult MRI study of trauma-exposed victims with and without PTSD, the paper does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of GM volume comparing PTSD patients vs controls. The MRI analyses reported are within-group voxel-based correlations (P300 amplitude vs GM density) in the PTSD group (N=6 with MRI) and reference prior between-group findings in a separate publication. Therefore it fails the required inclusion criteria I3 (study-level between-group GM volume comparison) and I4 (whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast). It meets inclusion criteria I6 (trauma-exposed control group) and I7 (adult sample). It thus should be excluded under E10 (reports only within-group results without a qualifying between-group contrast). Full text appears complete.

This is a treatment (CBT) study that uses voxel-based morphometry and reports pretreatment rACC volume correlations with treatment outcome and contrasts between PTSD subgroups (responders vs nonresponders) and control groups. However, it does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD patients (as a combined group) versus controls. Therefore it fails the required inclusion criterion I4 and meets exclusion criterion E9 (treatment study without a qualifying PTSD vs control whole-brain contrast). Satisfied inclusion criteria: I3 (empirical English MRI study assessing GM volume), I5 (reports coordinates/figures for voxel-wise results), I6 (uses trauma-exposed and healthy controls), I7 (adult human sample). Not met: I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise PTSD vs control contrast). Consequently, exclude from the meta-analysis.

Exclusion ID met: E6 (paediatric/adolescent sample). Inclusion IDs met: I3 (empirical MRI study assessing GM volume differences), I4 (reports whole-brain voxel-wise VBM between-group contrasts), I5 (results presented in figures/tables), I6 (control population is trauma-exposed non-PTSD). Inclusion ID not met: I7 (sample restricted to adults) — this study’s sample is adolescents (mean age 15.15 years, range 8–19), so does not meet the adult-sample requirement. Full text appears complete. Therefore the study must be excluded from this adult PTSD morphometry meta-analysis.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare gray matter between PTSD patients and controls (fire survivors). It reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts with Talairach coordinates, SPM maps, and a table of significant loci (left hippocampus, left ACC, bilateral insula). Controls are trauma-exposed individuals without PTSD; sample are adults (mean ages ~34). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion and therefore appears complete. All required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical, English-language MRI study of adults that used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to perform whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts comparing recent-onset PTSD patients to trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls. The paper reports significant GM volume decreases (coordinates and figures/tables provided) in left hippocampus and bilateral calcarine cortex, satisfying the requirement for whole-brain voxel-wise results. Both groups are adult miners (mean ages >18). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not pediatric, not non-empirical, includes a qualifying between-group contrast with positive findings). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete.
